topic: Winter electricity demand against the forecast
decision: whether to buy 40 MW of extra peak capacity for this winter

columns.forecast_peak_mw: day-ahead forecast of peak demand, MW
columns.available_capacity_mw: generating capacity available that day, MW
columns.imports_mw: power bought from neighbouring grids at the peak, MW
columns.residential_share_pct: share of peak demand from homes, percent

findings.text: Across all 90 days the forecast was off by 1.3% on average.
Wind speed has almost no relation to peak demand (correlation -0.02).
The forecast under-predicts demand on very cold days. On the 7 days below −15 °C, actual peak demand was 5.3% above the forecast on average (about 47 MW).
Weekend peaks are about 12% lower than weekday peaks.
The share of demand from homes rises in cold weather.
Peak demand exceeded available capacity on 4 days, 12 to 15 January, and the shortfall was covered with emergency imports.
Imports at the daily peak averaged 22 MW.
Unit 3 (50 MW) was out for repair from 10 to 16 January, cutting available capacity from 960 to 910 MW. With Unit 3 running, only 14 January would have exceeded capacity.
The highest peak of the winter was 1,012 MW on 14 January.
On mild days (above −3 °C) the forecast slightly over-predicts, by 1.8% on average.

main.gist: Demand outruns the forecast on very cold days and exceeded capacity in the January cold snap

caveat.gist: Unit 3 was out for repair, so capacity was 50 MW lower that week

facts.q: On the coldest days, by roughly what percentage did actual peak demand exceed the forecast?
On how many days did peak demand exceed the available capacity?
